# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-16 (Extended v127)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826. **Current narrative point (Spring Year 4—Louis Philippe's reign, April 1832)**: Paris—Gorbeau house (50-52, Salpêtrière district); Luxembourg gardens; le Petit-Picpus convent; M. Gillenormand's residences; wine-shops in Faubourg Saint-Antoine; English provincial towns (Dunstead, Staveford, Kelmere, Torton, Ostcombe, Ravenmere, Kelford, Yarlby, Gulhaven, Wilwick, Wilholt, Quenford). **Environmental details**: Rain threatened; frost silvered hedges; wind carries salt/tar scent; bees hum in lavender; children chase hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; smoke from chimneys lies flat; gulls quarrel over fish heads in harbor towns. Bells ring for vespers. Light goes early.

## Primary Locations
**GORBEAU HOUSE**: 50-52 Salpêtrière district. **JONDRETTE DEN**: Abject, fetid. Furniture: straw chair, infirm table, two pallets, straw beds. Walls: leprous, seamed, charcoal sketches, moisture. Fireplace with red-hot brazier. Dormer window (four broken panes). Colored engraving "THE DREAM" (Napoleon on blue column). **Wooden panel—Battle of Waterloo**: sergeant rescuer (Thénardier) carrying colonel victim (Pontmercy). Rope-ladder with hooks, verdigris candlestick.

**WINE-SHOPS (FAUBOURG SAINT-ANTOINE)**: Centers of revolutionary fermentation. Men openly discuss cartridge-making, plot readiness, armed resistance. Bourgeois visitors in good coats arrive, shake hands with "important" men, depart within ten minutes. Patriotic women embrace newcomers. Meetings sometimes periodic (8-10 persons, always same) or open (room so full must stand). Attendance mixed: some from enthusiasm, some merely passing to work. Wine-shop near point Saint-Eustache suspected as meeting place for "principal leaders." Aug—, chief of Society aid for tailors, Rue Mondétour, serves as intermediary between leaders and Faubourg Saint-Antoine.

## Crisis at Gorbeau House: Resolution
**M. Leblanc's binding and struggle**: Remained impassive despite brutal assault. Overturned furniture, moved toward window. Despite binding, preserved silence, forgot anxiety for own life.

**Thénardier's metamorphosis**: Transformed from ferocious robber into polished negotiator. Devised scheme: wife to dress as before, hunt up "the Lark" (Cosette) with letter from M. Leblanc. Girl will follow into carriage; outside barrier, trap with two horses waits. Young lady will be taken by comrade in other vehicle; wife returns to report. **Threat**: "If you have me arrested, my comrade will give a turn of his thumb to the Lark." Avoided naming girl—precaution of clever man.

**M. Leblanc's extraordinary escape (turning point)**: Concealed coin piece when searched; unscrewed and used as saw to cut cords (explaining faint noise Marius observed). Before seven men could act, stretched hand to brazier. **Brandished above his head the red-hot chisel, emitting threatening glow**. All huddled in amazement. While red-hot iron sank into smoking wound, **impassive and almost august, he fixed on Thénardier his beautiful glance, in which there was no hatred, and where suffering vanished in serene majesty.**

**Javert's ambush and final escape**: Javert (tall man, square face, thin firm mouth, thick gray whiskers) positioned outside with men. Grew impatient, took action before Marius's signal. Ruffians terrified, seized abandoned arms (meat-axe, key, bludgeon, shears, pincers, hammers). Thénardier had knife. **Thénardier woman snatched enormous paving-stone, hurled at Javert's head; Javert ducked; stone struck wall behind.** **M. Leblanc's escape**: Took advantage of confusion, darkness, diverted attention. Dashed out window (door guarded, but window was not).

## Marius Pontmercy: Crisis of Conscience (Unresolved)
**Identity and age**: Baron Marius Pontmercy, twenty years old; three years estranged from grandfather. **Paternal legacy**: Colonel's written instruction regarding Waterloo sergeant Thénardier. Recognized Thénardier in Waterloo painting.

**Unprecedented perplexity**: For last hour, two voices in conscience—one enjoining respect for father's testament, other crying to rescue prisoner. Extraordinary moral dilemma: everything depended on Marius. If he fired pistol, M. Leblanc saved, Thénardier lost; if not, M. Leblanc sacrificed. Father once saved by Thénardier at Waterloo. Yet M. Leblanc now victim of Thénardier's ambush. Moral obligation to both. **Crisis outcome unclear.**

## Girl (Cosette) and M. Leblanc Identity
**Girl identity clarified**: Handkerchief bore letters U. F., meaning Urbain Fabre. M. Leblanc is Monsieur Fabre—girl's biological father. Cosette became convent scholar; believes Valjean is her father. Marius recognizes: the "girl" he worshipped is Cosette, Thénardier's captive held for ransom scheme.

## Jean Valjean
Valjean integrated as convent assistant gardener; inhabits old garden hut with Fauchelevent. Spiritual transformation complete. Fauchelevent sole ally aware of full presence.

## English Provincial Towns: Population Movements and Daily Life
**Population movements**: Peten Haskick moved to Quenford; Lura Haskick followed. Kadrek moved to Wilholt. Zalis Corrley's daughter settled Wilholt. Kadan Corrley took Yewyn Corrford in marriage at Kelmere. Quiet Jotho married eldest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth at Ostcombe; couple lived there. **That spring, coughing sickness took Nelan; buried at Kelford.** Families involved: Stenworth, Prydenridge, Thornmere, Lindmere, Brackick.

**Daily mundane activities**: Sorting old letters, mending torn sleeves, scrubbing steps, humming childhood tunes. Fewyn Stenworth and Rorald argued with carter over oats price. Thizek argued with carter over sack of oats. Pelia Lindmere and Havie Prydenridge read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Luena Stenenridge read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Nerine mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Volan watched clouds, predicted rain wrongly. Volia hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Luena Stenenridge gave jade mirror to Rozek. Rozek complained of aching back. Luena laughed at story nobody else found funny. Kassa Brackick counted coins twice, came up penny short. Weather, harvest, river conditions constant conversation topics.

## Historical Context: The Restoration, Revolution of July, and Current Fermentation (1815-1832)
**Bourbon Restoration critique**: House of Bourbon returned after Napoleon fell. Believed it bestowed rights and could take back charter rights. Did not understand roots of French society not fixed in Bourbons but in nations.

**Restoration's fatal decision (1830)**: Contested collective title and individual right of nation to sovereignty, citizen to liberty. Denied to nation that which made it a nation.

**Fifteen years of intellectual progress (1815-1830)**: Great principles—equality before law, liberty of conscience, speech, press—worked in perfect peace. Bourbons were instrument of civilization which broke in Providence's hands.

**Revolution of July (1830)**: Hardly produced shock; did not treat vanquished royalty as enemy. Mysterious respect springs from events where we sense collaboration of someone working above man.

**Philosophical reflection on Right vs. Fact**: Property of right eternally beautiful and pure. Fact containing little right destined to become deformed, impure, monstrous.

**Louis Philippe (Winter/Spring Year 4)**: Handsome in old age, remained graceful; not always approved by nation, always by masses. Lacked majesty; wore no crown, no white hair. Mixture of noble and bourgeois suited 1830. Incorruptible; went out with umbrella. Bit of mason, gardener, doctor. Royalists jeered—first king to shed blood with object of healing. Policy domestic rather than national; excessive timidity displeasing to people. Deep tenderness toward family. One daughter, Marie d'Orleans, placed race among artists. Press free, tribune free, conscience and speech free. **What can be said: Louis Philippe, from point of view of human goodness, will remain one of best princes who ever sat on throne.** Moments when overwhelmed by difficulties of being king.

**Cloud gathering (Spring Year 4)**: Strange shade gradually drew nearer, extended over men, things, ideas—shade from wraths and systems. Everything hastily stifled, moving, fermenting. Piles of shadows covered horizon. Electric tension such that first comer, stranger, brought light. Deep and dull mutterings allowed judgment of quantity of thunder contained by cloud. **Ever since 1830, petty partial revolts suppressed but ever bursting forth afresh—sign of vast underlying conflagration.**

## Revolutionary Fermentation and Secret Societies (Spring 1832)
**Wine-shop agitation**: Workmen openly proclaim cartridge-making. "In less than a fortnight we shall be parallel with the government. With twenty-five thousand men we can face them." "I don't sleep at night, because I make cartridges all night." Soldiers' arms coveted: "The soldiers have!" Remarks exchanged in low tone: "The plot is ripe, the matter is arranged." Exaltation such one workman exclaimed: "We have no arms!"

**Public signs of conspiracy**: Woman sweeping doorsteps remarks: "For a long time, there has been a strong force busy making cartridges." Proclamations addressed to National Guard in departments signed by _Burtot, wine-merchant_. Passages most deeply moving to crowd: **"Our doctrines are trammelled, our proclamations torn, our bill-stickers spied upon and thrown into prison."** **"The future of nations is being worked out in our obscure ranks."** **"Action or reaction, revolution or counter-revolution. For the people against the people, that is the question."** **"On the day when we cease to suit you, break us, but up to that day, help us to march on."** All in broad daylight.

**Suspicious activities**: April 4, 1832, passer-by mounted post at corner of Rue Sainte-Marguerite, shouted: "I am a Babouvist!" But beneath Babeuf, people scented Gisquet. At nightfall, workman encountered near canal by "very well dressed man" warned: "Don't be alarmed, I am an agent of the committee. You are suspected of not being quite faithful. If you reveal anything, there is an eye fixed on you." Man shook hands and departed saying: "We shall meet again soon."

**Discovered documents**: Mason returning from work left package on bench near bridge of Austerlitz. Found: two printed dialogues signed _Lahautière_, song "Workmen, band together," tin box full cartridges. In ditch between Père-Lachaise and Barrière du Trône, children discovered: bag containing bullet-mould, wooden punch for cartridge preparation, wooden bowl with hunting-powder grains, cast-iron pot with melted lead traces.

**The cipher document (April 15, 1832)**: Carpenter picked up torn papers; one extremely significant. Document bore: Q, C, D, E with instruction: "Learn this list by heart. After so doing you will tear it up. The men admitted will do the same when you have transmitted their orders to them. Health and Fraternity, u og a' fe L." **Letters meant: quinturions, centurions, decurions, éclaireurs [scouts]; date u og a' fe = April 15, 1832.** Under each capital letter: names with characteristic notes. Q. _Bannerel_. 8 guns, 83 cartridges. Safe man.—C. _Boubière_. 1 pistol, 40 cartridges.—D. _Rollet_. 1 foil, 1 pistol, 1 pound powder.—E. _Tessier_. 1 sword, 1 cartridge-box. Exact.— _Terreur_. 8 guns. Brave.

**Unité document**: Lists names and locations—Blanchard: Arbre-Sec. Barra. Soize. Salle-au-Comte. Kosciusko. Aubry Butcher. J.J.R. Caius Gracchus. Dufond. Derbac. Maubuée. Washington. Pinson. Michel. Quincampoix. Hoche. Marceau. Plato. Warsaw. Tilly, crier of Populaire. Complete nomenclature of sections of fourth arrondissement of Society of Rights of Man, with names and dwellings of section chiefs. Foundation of Society appears posterior to document date; possibly only rough draft.
